item.title: Keeping my Mac setup reproducible
item.description: How I use Homebrew, mise and chezmoi to manage and rebuild my Mac setup.
item.content:encoded:
I've become weirdly happy with my Mac setup. I can describe how to rebuild it without relying on a memory of everything I've installed over the years.

Three tools have clear jobs: Homebrew installs Mac apps and system packages, mise manages developer tools, and chezmoi manages my dotfiles and setup scripts.

It's the same idea I liked in server bootstrap tooling: the machine shouldn't be a mystery. I'd accepted that for servers years ago, while still treating my laptop as something assembled by hand and repaired from memory.

Give each tool a job​

For my setup, the split is:

ToolWhat I use it for
HomebrewDesktop apps, system packages, fonts and bootstrap tools
miseLanguage runtimes, formatters and developer CLIs
chezmoiShell configuration, aliases, editor defaults, package inventories and setup scripts

There's overlap in what these tools can do. The useful part is choosing an owner for each piece so I don't install the same thing through several routes.

When I need a Mac app, I reach for Homebrew. When I need a project runtime, I reach for mise. When I change how my shell behaves, I change the chezmoi source.

That's easier to follow than "I probably installed this with whatever the README told me in 2021."

Keep the developer toolchain in one place​

I already wrote about managing runtimes and tasks with mise. Here, the benefit is knowing where developer tools belong.

The exact tools change. The ownership rule stays the same. A new formatter or command-line utility goes into the toolchain configuration rather than becoming another installer command I need to remember.

Pinning versions gives you more control over rebuilds. Using latest is a choice to accept newer releases when installing, rather than a guarantee that a fresh machine will get the same versions.

Review configuration before applying it​

chezmoi gives me a simple workflow:

chezmoi diff
chezmoi apply
chezmoi status

I can see the proposed changes, apply them, then inspect differences between the managed files and their target state. This covers the files chezmoi manages; it isn't a health check for the entire machine.

Templates let me share configuration without assuming every machine is identical. Machine-specific values can live outside the public source. Secrets need their own handling, rather than being committed as template values.

The shell setup is where I notice the difference most. Bash and zsh can share common interactive behaviour. Aliases have a home, PATH setup is deliberate, and the rc files become entry points rather than junk drawers.

Instead of asking, "Which file did I hack this into?", I can ask, "Which tool owns this?"

Check the result​

One of my favourite pieces is a small doctor script that runs after applying changes. It checks whether expected tools are reachable, whether package inventories have drifted and whether managed files match what I expect.

It doesn't prove the whole setup is correct. It turns some common failures into a list I can act on, which is better than opening a terminal and vaguely feeling that something's off.

The cost is maintenance​

I still have to review changes, update the source and keep the boundary between the three tools clear. Pasting a random installer into a shell startup file can undo that clarity quite quickly.

I'd rather maintain a visible configuration than a vague memory of how the machine became useful. The aim is to make the important parts repeatable, without automating every preference I might ever have.

The old infrastructure saying is that servers should be cattle, not pets. My laptop is personal enough that I don't quite want that. A well-documented pet will do: it has my preferences, but if it disappears tomorrow, I have a map for rebuilding it.

item.title: Benchmarking Docling on the wrong hardware
item.description: We compared ten document parsers, chose the one that best preserved our documents, and then found it was too slow on our production hardware.
item.content:encoded:
We compared ten document parsers, chose the one that best preserved our documents, and then found it was too slow on our production hardware.

The evaluation helped us choose for extraction quality. It didn't tell us enough about the environment where the parser would run.

What we needed to preserve​

Our assistant retrieved content from product documentation: policies, guides and structured forms. The quality of that retrieval depended on what survived parsing.

A table flattened into unrelated values loses meaning. So does a heading treated as an ordinary paragraph or a caption separated from its figure. Those defects affect what the assistant can retrieve and cite.

Our document set needed support for:

  • Scanned PDFs requiring optical character recognition (OCR).
  • Tables with merged cells and multi-row headers.
  • Heading hierarchy, columns and other layout structure.
  • Figures and diagrams whose meaning needed to be captured in text.

We started with python-docx, pdfplumber, pypdf and PyMuPDF. They were useful for parts of the problem, but our initial approaches didn't preserve enough structure across the more difficult documents.

Making the comparison repeatable​

We built a comparison harness to run parsers against the same input documents. We measured parse time and peak memory, then compared text extraction, table structure and layout quality.

Word count was one proxy for text extraction, not proof that the content was correct. The qualitative review mattered too: a parser could return plenty of words and still lose the relationships between them.

In that evaluation, Docling best met the extraction requirements we cared about. We integrated it.

The hardware gap​

We had run the evaluation on an M4 Pro MacBook with Apple Silicon MPS acceleration. Our production Kubernetes nodes were CPU-only.

In our tests, documents that parsed in two or three seconds on the laptop could take minutes in a production pod. Our load balancer's 60-second timeout made that a request-path problem, not just a slower batch job.

We saw timeouts, 502 responses, retries, backlog and memory pressure. Several weeks of thread and concurrency tuning followed. The Docling removal post covers that work.

Those timings describe our setup and document set. They aren't a general CPU-versus-GPU benchmark. But they were enough to show that our original evaluation hadn't answered the deployment question.

The harness made comparisons consistent. We had still chosen the wrong environment for a performance measurement that mattered.

Reconsidering the approach​

We could have evaluated GPU nodes, moved parsing behind an asynchronous job or spent more time tuning the local pipeline. Each would have changed the cost and behaviour of the system.

Instead, we reconsidered whether inference needed to run locally at all. The requirement was to extract structured content from documents. Local inference had been our implementation choice.

We tried Claude through Bedrock. Documents within the direct-input limit went to the API as document blocks. Larger files used a fallback that rendered pages as images. AWS documents the Converse message limits, including 4.5 MB per document.

On our document set, the extraction quality was comparable to what we'd been getting from Docling. Moving inference out of the pods removed the local model loading and CPU tuning from that path.

It introduced different considerations: provider availability, quotas, per-request cost, data handling and output quality. For our system, that was a better trade-off.

What I'd add to the evaluation​

Run on representative hardware. If a library performs inference locally, test it under the CPU, memory, accelerator and concurrency constraints it will actually have. Laptop timings can help development without being deployment evidence.

Measure the complete operation. Include startup, model downloads or loading, realistic document sizes, timeouts and concurrent requests where those affect the design.

Compare different approaches. Asking which local library is best excludes managed services before you've considered their trade-offs. Include plausible alternatives, then assess them against the same extraction and operational requirements.

Keep evaluation and decision separate. A harness reports what you measured. Deciding that a tool fits the system still requires judgement about what you left out.

I'd keep the structured comparison. I'd change the questions it had to answer before we committed to the result.

item.title: Why we removed Docling
item.description: We spent five weeks integrating and tuning Docling, then removed it. The removal deleted 1,452 lines from uv.lock alone.
item.content:encoded:
We spent five weeks integrating and tuning Docling, then removed it. The removal deleted 1,452 lines from uv.lock alone.

The parser met our document-extraction requirements. Running its models inside our application pods cost more operational work than we'd expected, and a managed API eventually met the need with less local infrastructure.

Adding the parser​

Docling handles document conversion, including PDFs, tables and Word documents. Our integration also brought model downloads, OCR dependencies and inference into the application runtime.

The first pull request was merged and reverted on the same day. That should probably have earned more attention than it did.

A couple of days later, the integration was back. We needed to:

  • Download Hugging Face models during container startup.
  • Set HOME and HF_HOME so the container could write to its cache.
  • Fix how the DOCLING_MODELS list passed through shell arguments.
  • Add Tesseract OCR and OpenCV to the runtime image.
  • Keep EasyOCR out of the model list when it wasn't part of the intended setup.

Each issue was manageable. Together, they were a sign that we'd taken on more than a parsing function.

Managing the models​

Downloading models during startup was too slow for our production health checks. We introduced a CI workflow to prepare them in the image, then moved towards an S3 cache and a Kubernetes init container as image size became a problem.

The model sync workflow had its own configuration and bugs. It also had to stay aligned with the Docling version in pyproject.toml. Updating the parser or OCR engine meant coordinating the Dockerfile, sync workflow and cached models before deployment.

We'd added a parsing library and ended up maintaining a model-distribution process.

Tuning the runtime​

Several rounds of changes followed:

  • Reduced the OpenMP thread count from four to two after CPU throttling.
  • Pinned images_scale to 1.0 and set the accelerator to AUTO.
  • Fixed thread initialisation and split up the parse method to make tuning easier.
  • Switched from EasyOCR to RapidOCR, then updated the model sync workflow and defaults.
  • Skipped OCR for native digital PDFs where it wasn't needed.

These changes addressed specific problems, but the operational cost kept growing.

On the day of the last round of fixes, we added a parser using a vision-language model (VLM) through Bedrock. We validated that route in a few hours. It removed local inference from the request path.

Removing the unused integration​

We changed the default routing to use the VLM parsers. Docling was still in the source, Docker image and dependency tree, but it was handling no traffic.

So we removed the parser, its tests, the model sync workflow, settings, entrypoint bootstrap and inference dependencies. That was where the 1,452-line lockfile reduction came from.

What replaced it​

The primary parser sends document bytes to Claude through Bedrock. For documents that exceed the direct-input limit, a fallback rasterises PDF pages with pypdfium2 and sends page images for extraction. DOCX files on that fallback route go through headless LibreOffice first.

AWS documents a 4.5 MB limit per document in Converse messages. The fallback also has to respect image, request and model limits; converting a file to images doesn't remove those constraints.

ConcernOur Docling integrationReplacement
Document extractionLocally loaded parser and OCR modelsBedrock document input, with a page-image fallback
Model distributionS3 sync workflow and startup configurationManaged by the provider
Local dependenciesTorch, OCR engines, OpenCV and model filespypdfium2 and LibreOffice for the fallback
Runtime concernsModel loading, memory, CPU and thread tuningAPI latency, quotas, cost and failure handling

We removed one set of responsibilities and accepted another. The managed route still needs monitoring, retries where appropriate, and review of what document data can be sent to the provider.

What I'd check earlier​

Our mistake was treating extraction quality as enough evidence to commit to the integration. We hadn't adequately checked what it would take to operate the chosen pipeline on CPU-limited production pods.

That doesn't establish that Docling needs a GPU or can't run well on a CPU. Its configuration options and the workload matter. We may have missed settings that would have helped.

A managed API also isn't an option everywhere. Self-hosting, offline processing and data-handling constraints can justify the work of operating local models.

For our workload and environment, the API route met the need with less local operational work. I'd compare that option earlier next time, alongside testing the local parser on production-equivalent hardware.

item.title: What to leave out of an architecture diagram
item.description: There's a particular type of diagram that engineers love producing and nobody can read. Boxes for every service, arrows for every dependency, and a legend that requires its own legend. The details may all be accurate, but you still can't tell what the system does.
item.content:encoded:
There's a particular type of diagram that engineers love producing and nobody can read. Boxes for every service, arrows for every dependency, and a legend that requires its own legend. The details may all be accurate, but you still can't tell what the system does.

A useful architecture diagram answers a question for its reader. Deciding what to leave out is part of that job.

I've been doing C4 modelling for a while, and that's what I like about it. System Context, Container, Component, Code: four levels of detail for different questions and audiences. Mixing those levels makes it harder to see what a diagram is trying to explain.

The tooling has been a headache. I tried a few diagram-as-code options that seemed to get in the way more than they helped. I've recently switched to D2, and it's been noticeably better for me. The syntax is small, the output is clean, and I can spend more time on what the diagram needs to say.

What question does the diagram answer?​

Engineers instinctively want to put everything in. Every dependency. Every call. Every integration they personally wired up at 11pm on a Thursday and feel a certain proprietary affection for.

Those details can matter. If you're debugging how a chat request moves through the system, protocols, authentication and session storage are relevant:

But if someone asks, "What are the main parts of this chat application?", the request-level detail gets in the way. A simpler view helps:

The first view helps trace a request. The second shows the broad responsibilities: the web app sends messages to an API, which calls a language-model provider and stores conversations.

These are illustrative sketches, not equivalent views of a fully specified system. The second deliberately leaves out authentication, caching and the gateway. Those need to appear in another view if they're relevant to the reader's question. A full C4 container diagram would also show the system boundary, major technology choices and how the applications and data stores communicate.

Removing detail is useful only if the remaining picture still answers the question accurately.

Give AI tools the same brief​

AI tools can make the arrows problem worse. Ask for an architecture diagram without saying who it's for or what it needs to explain, and you can end up with every import, function call and database relationship the tool can find.

That might help you investigate dependencies. It won't necessarily help a new team member understand the system.

Tell the tool the audience, the question and the level of detail. Review what it leaves out as carefully as what it includes. Access to the code doesn't tell it which relationships matter for this particular explanation.

I prefer top-down layouts because I find them easier to scan. But layout comes after scope. Neatly arranging too much detail still leaves you with too much detail.

The test I use: can someone new to the team look at the diagram and explain the part of the system it covers, without me hovering over their shoulder narrating? If they need me to explain the diagram first, I've drawn a very expensive set of notes.

item.title: Enforcing architecture rules in CI
item.description: Two engineers can review the same pull request and disagree about where the code belongs. They may have worked in the same repository for months without realising they have different ideas about its architecture.
item.content:encoded:
Two engineers can review the same pull request and disagree about where the code belongs. They may have worked in the same repository for months without realising they have different ideas about its architecture.

We've caught that kind of drift with architecture tests: checks that turn agreed dependency rules into failures in continuous integration (CI).

Different projects and professional backgrounds teach different habits. Unless a team makes its boundaries explicit, those habits become assumptions that surface during code review.

pytest-archon lets you express import rules for a Python codebase. For example, suppose the team has agreed that API modules must not import database modules directly:

from pytest_archon import archrule


def test_api_does_not_import_database():
    (
        archrule("api-layer-isolation", use_regex=True)
        .match(r"^myapp\.api(\..*)?$")
        .should_not_import(r"^myapp\.database(\..*)?$")
        .check("myapp", only_direct_imports=True)
    )

The patterns include the package modules themselves and their submodules. only_direct_imports=True limits this rule to direct imports; without it, pytest-archon also checks transitive dependencies.

Run the test in CI and an API handler that imports a database model will fail the check. It won't prevent every possible way of reaching the database at runtime. It checks the import boundary we've described.

The same feedback for humans and agents​

An agent doesn't automatically know that your team agreed on this boundary six months ago. Written instructions help, but an executable check also tells it when its change violates the rule.

That's useful for human contributors too. A visible, consistently checked rule can reduce the time spent repeating the same dependency discussion in review.

The test doesn't decide whether the boundary is right. The team still needs to agree on it, explain why it matters and change it when the design changes. Architecture tests can enforce a poor decision just as reliably as a good one.

What they give us is a way to catch divergence early, before different assumptions become established patterns across the repository.

item.title: Tracing a Bedrock application with OpenTelemetry
item.description: A request takes twelve seconds. Was the time spent retrieving context, building the prompt, waiting for Bedrock or processing the response?
item.content:encoded:
A request takes twelve seconds. Was the time spent retrieving context, building the prompt, waiting for Bedrock or processing the response?

We hit this early on an LLM project. A single request duration wasn't enough to tell us where to look. Tracing the steps around the model call made the delay easier to investigate.

Trace the code you control​

Amazon Bedrock runs the model, but retrieval, prompt assembly, retries and fallback handling are still part of your application. Those steps don't need to be a mystery just because inference happens elsewhere.

I used OpenTelemetry spans to make those boundaries visible. A span records an operation's timing and can carry attributes and error information. Nested spans show how the work fits together.

For Python 3.10 or later, a small decorator can help with synchronous functions and methods:

import functools
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import ParamSpec, TypeVar

from opentelemetry import trace

Parameters = ParamSpec("Parameters")
Result = TypeVar("Result")


def traced(
    tracer: trace.Tracer,
) -> Callable[[Callable[Parameters, Result]], Callable[Parameters, Result]]:
    def decorate(
        function: Callable[Parameters, Result],
    ) -> Callable[Parameters, Result]:
        @functools.wraps(function)
        def wrapper(*args: Parameters.args, **kwargs: Parameters.kwargs) -> Result:
            with tracer.start_as_current_span(function.__qualname__):
                return function(*args, **kwargs)

        return wrapper

    return decorate

Configure the OpenTelemetry SDK and exporter at application startup, then pass a tracer to the decorator: @traced(trace.get_tracer(__name__)). The span context records timing and, by default, exceptions that escape the block. Calling the API without a configured recording provider won't give you an exported trace.

This wrapper doesn't handle coroutines or generators. For those, the span must cover the awaited work or stream consumption, rather than just the creation of a coroutine or iterator.

Read the request as a timeline​

Once the relevant steps were instrumented, we could distinguish time spent in retrieval, prompt assembly and the model call. That gave us somewhere specific to investigate instead of treating every slow request as a model problem.

A long model span tells you where time went. It doesn't, by itself, prove the cause. Model choice, prompt size, caching and provider behaviour still need separate investigation.

We also used OpenTelemetry for application metrics, including fallback use and prompt-cache hits. Those need deliberate instrumentation and an appropriate collection setup. A timing decorator doesn't automatically produce business metrics, and sampled traces aren't necessarily a reliable count of every request.

Keep raw prompts, retrieved documents and user content out of span attributes unless you have an explicit, appropriate data-handling policy. Useful tracing shouldn't depend on copying sensitive content into another system.

The model's output can still be difficult to explain. But we can make the surrounding application easier to inspect. I'd wire that in early, while the request path is still small enough to follow.

item.title: TDD makes code easier for agents to work with
item.description: The first time I set an agent loose on a real codebase, it ran out of context before it had done anything useful. That's a clarifying experience.
item.content:encoded:
The first time I set an agent loose on a real codebase, it ran out of context before it had done anything useful. That's a clarifying experience.

It was a Python monorepo with shared libraries and infrastructure code. I sketched the context window as a rectangle and filled in what the agent had loaded: the directory tree, instructions, modules, configuration and dependencies. More than half the space was gone before it reached the task.

A codebase with unclear boundaries, large modules and implicit conventions makes an agent spend its context working out where it is. A new engineer has the same orientation problem, but can build understanding over weeks. In the setup I was using, the agent started each session without that accumulated knowledge.

That made familiar engineering practices feel useful in a new way.

Tests give the agent somewhere to start​

Test-driven development (TDD) and the Extreme Programming (XP) practices around it encourage small steps, simple design and regular refactoring. When applied well, those practices can produce focused modules, explicit interfaces and tests that describe intended behaviour.

Those are useful properties when an agent can only hold part of a codebase in context.

A test called test_chat_service_returns_error_on_empty_prompt gives it a place to investigate the empty-prompt rule. It still needs to read the assertions and relevant implementation. But it has a starting point, rather than several hundred lines of service code to search without direction.

Tests also give feedback after a change. The agent doesn't have to infer every expectation from the current implementation, which might be the thing that's wrong.

This depends on the tests. A suite tied to private methods or incidental implementation details can make changes harder. Passing tests show that the checked expectations hold, not that the design is sound or every requirement is covered.

Structure reduces repeated investigation​

I've watched agents re-read files, trace implicit dependencies and rediscover conventions that could have been explicit. That costs time and context. With token-based billing, it can cost money too.

Small modules help when they have clear responsibilities. Splitting one confusing module into ten confusing files doesn't solve the problem.

Architecture tests can help with structural rules. If the API must not import database modules, make that expectation executable. Human and agent get the same feedback when a change crosses the boundary.

TDD doesn't guarantee that a codebase will be easy for agents to navigate. But the things I value in a testable codebase also help here: behaviour I can find, dependencies I can see and changes I can check without understanding the whole system first.

item.title: Walking skeletons for AI projects
item.description: I wrote about walking skeletons in 2021: get something small running end to end before going deep on features. It exposes permissions, deployment and infrastructure problems while there's still little code depending on your assumptions.
item.content:encoded:
I wrote about walking skeletons in 2021: get something small running end to end before going deep on features. It exposes permissions, deployment and infrastructure problems while there's still little code depending on your assumptions.

I've found the same approach useful on AI projects.

Model access, inference, data pipelines and evaluation each add things to connect. They can work in isolation and still fail when you put them together in the environment where the application needs to run.

On a recent AI project, we pushed to establish that path early. We hit IAM permissions that didn't behave as expected, model API access that needed a different approval route, and tooling that worked locally but failed in containers.

These were familiar delivery problems. Calling the project an AI project hadn't removed any of them.

AI tooling did help us work through them. Investigating IAM policies, drafting access requests and finding the right cloud configuration went faster with an assistant alongside. That's my experience on this project, rather than a guarantee about how quickly these problems can be fixed.

The walking skeleton gave us something concrete to investigate. Without trying the deployment, we wouldn't have known which assumptions were wrong.

The temptation to skip that step is still there. It's easy to get a prototype working and keep adding features before checking whether it can run in production. Faster code generation can leave you with more code waiting for a pipeline that doesn't exist yet.

For an AI application, I'd start with a thin path through the actual deployment and a real model call, using suitable test data. Then build out from something we know can run. It doesn't need to do much. It needs to expose the things that could stop us shipping.

item.title: Measuring time to first token
item.description: For a streaming chat response, total duration doesn't tell you how long the user stared at an empty screen.
item.content:encoded:
For a streaming chat response, total duration doesn't tell you how long the user stared at an empty screen.

I measure time to first token (TTFT) alongside total duration: in this test, the time from starting the request until the client receives the first non-empty piece of generated text.

That definition matters. A connection opening, a keep-alive or an event containing only metadata isn't the first token. The measurement also includes work outside model inference, such as the network and application processing. It isn't the same as timing when the browser actually paints the text.

Measure the first content event​

In k6's HTTP metrics, http_req_duration covers sending the request, waiting and receiving the response. It doesn't isolate the wait for generated text. http_req_waiting measures time to first byte, which may arrive before any useful content.

For an SSE endpoint, I've used xk6-sse. With Go and xk6 installed, this builds a k6 binary with the extension:

xk6 build --with github.com/phymbert/xk6-sse

The example below assumes a GET endpoint whose SSE data events contain JSON like {"content":"Hello"}, with [DONE] marking completion. Adapt the method, authentication and content extraction to your API; SSE itself doesn't define that payload format.

import sse from "k6/x/sse";
import { check } from "k6";
import { Trend } from "k6/metrics";

const ttft = new Trend("ttft_ms", true);

export default function () {
  const url = __ENV.STREAM_URL;
  const params = {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { Accept: "text/event-stream" },
  };
  const start = Date.now();
  let firstTokenRecorded = false;

  const response = sse.open(url, params, (client) => {
    client.on("event", (event) => {
      if (firstTokenRecorded || !event.data || event.data === "[DONE]") {
        return;
      }

      const payload = JSON.parse(event.data);
      if (typeof payload.content === "string" && payload.content.length > 0) {
        ttft.add(Date.now() - start);
        firstTokenRecorded = true;
      }
    });
  });

  check(response, {
    "stream returned 200": (result) => result.status === 200,
    "stream contained text": () => firstTokenRecorded,
  });
}

Time-valued k6 trends use milliseconds, so this records the elapsed milliseconds without dividing by 1,000. Run the resulting binary with your endpoint supplied as STREAM_URL.

The connection stays open after recording TTFT so the test still consumes the response. Closing it early would change the workload you're trying to observe.

Track errors, timeouts and streams with no text alongside TTFT. Those requests have no TTFT sample; a low percentile among successful streams can hide a failing service. The checks make some failures visible, but a real test also needs endpoint-specific error handling and failure thresholds.

Choose the load profile deliberately​

Ramping concurrency and holding at selected levels can help show where responsiveness changes. Keep the ramp and hold results distinguishable, and define whether you classify samples by request start or measurement time.

A 60-second hold with 50 virtual users doesn't imply 50 requests. Each user may complete several iterations. If you need one iteration per user, use a per-VU-iterations scenario and check how many iterations completed. That is a different experiment from sustaining concurrency for a fixed duration.

What we learnt​

In our tests, models differed in how quickly they started and how quickly they finished. Prompt-cache hits reduced the first-token delay by hundreds of milliseconds for large system prompts. We also saw TTFT degrade as concurrency increased before throughput alone made the problem obvious.

Those were observations from our workload, not performance guarantees for another model or deployment.

Before testing, choose a p95 TTFT target at the concurrency you expect, along with an acceptable error rate. Keep measuring total duration and token throughput too. A quick first token is useful, but it doesn't tell you whether the rest of the response arrives at a useful pace.

item.title: Managing runtimes and tasks with mise
item.description: You clone a repo you haven't touched in six months. The README says Python 3.11. You have 3.12. Before writing any code, you're working out which version manager the project uses and how to run its checks.
item.content:encoded:
You clone a repo you haven't touched in six months. The README says Python 3.11. You have 3.12. Before writing any code, you're working out which version manager the project uses and how to run its checks.

I use mise to keep runtime versions and project tasks in one place.

The problem isn't limited to Python. Switching projects can mean switching between pyenv, nvm, tfenv, Makefiles and shell scripts. Each can work well, but you still need to discover the conventions for the repo in front of you.

Versions and tasks in one file​

For a Python project with pytest already installed in its project environment, a small mise.toml might look like this:

[tools]
python = "3.12.3"

[tasks.test]
description = "Run the test suite"
run = "pytest"

[tasks.verify]
description = "Run all project checks"
depends = ["test"]

The Python version is illustrative; use a supported version that your project has agreed on. The config doesn't install pytest or the application dependencies. Keep the project's environment setup explicit too.

Review the file before trusting the project configuration, then run:

mise trust
mise install
mise tasks
mise run verify

mise tasks lists the available tasks. mise run verify gives contributors a consistent command, even if the checks behind it change.

The task dependency rules matter: dependencies can run in parallel. Listing test and build in depends doesn't mean that one finishes before the other starts.

Hide the mechanics behind a useful command​

One project needed a custom k6 binary for testing a streaming API. Building it involved Go, xk6 and an SSE extension. The build task ran:

xk6 build --with github.com/phymbert/xk6-sse

Wrapping that in a task gave the team one command to remember. It didn't remove the prerequisites: the project still needed to install and pin Go and xk6, as well as the extension version if we wanted repeatable builds.

That's the useful distinction. A task can hide the mechanics at the call site while keeping them visible in the repository.

Use the same task in CI​

The same approach works in GitHub Actions:

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: jdx/mise-action@v4
      - run: mise run verify

This is the task-running part of a workflow, not a complete application setup. Add the project's dependency installation before verification. The action versions shown are an example; review and pin the versions you use.

Sharing the command and tool configuration reduces one source of drift between local development and CI. It doesn't make their operating systems, services or environment variables identical.

Bootstrap the machine separately​

mise needs to be installed before it can manage a project. I handle that through chezmoi, which manages my dotfiles and bootstrap scripts. The shell configuration activates mise for interactive use:

eval "$(mise activate zsh)"

chezmoi handles my machine setup; mise handles the developer toolchain and project commands. Keeping those responsibilities clear has been more useful than trying to make one tool own everything.

I wouldn't migrate a settled nvm and make project just to standardise it for its own sake. For me, the benefit comes from switching between projects without having to rediscover how each one works.

item.title: A VS Code snippet for Markdown front matter
item.description: I use a VS Code snippet to add the front matter for a post on this blog.
item.content:encoded:
I use a VS Code snippet to add the front matter for a post on this blog.

  1. Open Snippets: Configure Snippets from the Command Palette.
  2. Choose New Global Snippets file and give it a name.
  3. Add the JSON below.
  4. In a Markdown file, run Insert Snippet and choose Add Docusaurus blog front matter, or type frontmatter and select the completion when offered.
{
  "Add Docusaurus blog front matter": {
    "scope": "markdown,mdx",
    "prefix": "frontmatter",
    "description": "Add draft post metadata for this blog",
    "body": [
      "---",
      "draft: true",
      "date: ${1:YYYY-MM-DDT00:00:00.000Z}",
      "title: \"${2:Post title}\"",
      "slug: ${TM_FILENAME_BASE}",
      "authors: [ambersariya]",
      "tags:",
      "  - ${3:tag}",
      "---",
      "",
      "$0"
    ]
  }
}

Name the file in kebab case, such as my-new-post.md; the snippet uses that name without the extension as the slug. Use Tab to move through the date, title and tag fields.

Replace the date placeholder with a real UTC timestamp. The trailing Z means UTC; appending it to VS Code's local-time variables would mislabel the time.

The author key is specific to this site. Change it for another blog, and review the metadata before removing draft: true.

item.title: Start with a walking skeleton
item.description: I've been reading Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests. One idea I wish I'd applied sooner is the walking skeleton: a small implementation that connects the main parts of a system and can be deployed end to end.
item.content:encoded:
I've been reading Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests. One idea I wish I'd applied sooner is the walking skeleton: a small implementation that connects the main parts of a system and can be deployed end to end.

It's tempting to start a new project by solving the interesting problem in code and leave deployment until later. I've done that. We built an application locally, intending to put it online when the first feature was ready.

When we tried, we hit security policies, technology restrictions and release processes we hadn't accounted for. Sorting them out took a couple of months of back and forth between development, operations and administration teams.

We knew there were constraints. Deferring the details seemed reasonable until those details stopped us releasing anything.

A walking skeleton would have given us that feedback earlier. Even a hello-world application passing through the real deployment process would have forced us to deal with access, infrastructure and release approvals before building features around untested assumptions.

That's what I'd tell my past self: get something small running end to end, then build on it. A working application on your laptop hasn't proved that you can release it.

item.title: Journey to the centre of the stack
item.description: Containerising legacy software has always been a journey into the unknown. What's changed is who you take with you.
item.content:encoded:
I first wrote this post in 2020 after spending several weeks containerising a legacy application I hadn't built and didn't fully understand. It was mostly archaeology: reading old configuration, tracing hardcoded paths and figuring out what half a dozen processes did before touching anything. By the time I had a working Docker image, I'd earned it.

I'd approach parts of that work differently now, with AI tools helping me investigate the code. The decisions still need just as much care.

Getting oriented​

Working in unfamiliar legacy code takes concentration. Before you can decide what to change, you need to understand what you're looking at.

An agent can help map dependencies, find uses of a configuration value, summarise a module or trace what happens to an uploaded file. Those answers need checking, but they can give you a starting point faster than opening files without a clear route through them.

That leaves more time for the architectural questions: where state belongs, how processes interact and which assumptions a container will break.

What the code doesn't tell you​

A hardcoded path might look easy to replace with an environment variable. But the code won't necessarily tell you about the cron job on the production server that expects files at that path.

The same problem applies to session storage, deployment defaults and shared directories. Some choices reflect constraints that still exist. Others are leftovers. You need evidence before deciding which is which.

An agent can only use the context it has. Deployment constraints, team agreements and the reasons behind old decisions may be missing from the repository. Talk to the people who know the system and check the running environment where you can.

Finding a dependency is useful. Establishing that it's safe to change is a separate job.

How I'd approach it now​

Map the application first. Find the processes, configuration files, external services and hardcoded paths. Use an agent's summary to guide investigation, then verify the important relationships. A static read won't reveal every runtime behaviour.

Identify the decisions. Session handling, persistent storage, secrets and multiple running instances need deliberate choices. Get those questions in front of the people who can answer them before spending days polishing the Dockerfile.

Keep the image straightforward. A common base image can help when several applications share a runtime and need the same updates. Don't introduce one just because the Dockerfiles look similar.

Make environment-specific configuration explicit. Paths, service URLs and feature flags need a clear configuration mechanism. Supply secrets through the deployment platform's secret mechanism; don't bake them into the image.

Run the application early. Build a small working container, find the first failure, fix it and repeat. Check behaviour at the boundaries you're changing, especially storage and process startup.

Account for dependencies. Every system library, OCR engine or local model becomes part of what you build, update and operate. Our Docling experience is a reminder of how much work can hide behind adding one package.

The journey to the centre of the stack still involves unfamiliar code and decisions with consequences. Better tools can reduce the reading needed to reach those decisions. They don't remove the need to understand them.

item.title: JSON Web Tokens
item.content:encoded:
A JSON Web Token (JWT) carries claims between systems. A claim is a statement, such as who a token represents or when it expires.

A signed token lets a receiver check its integrity and that it was created by someone holding the signing key. That doesn't make the claims confidential, or make every action described by them authorised.

What a signed token contains​

A common signed JWT uses three base64url-encoded parts, separated by dots:

header.payload.signature

For example, the decoded header might be:

{
  "alg": "HS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}

And the payload:

{
  "sub": "1234567890",
  "name": "John Doe",
  "admin": true
}

The signature covers the encoded header and payload. With HS256, it uses HMAC-SHA256 and a shared secret. Other algorithms use a private key to sign and a public key to verify. Use a maintained library rather than implementing this yourself. The signed format is defined in RFC 7515.

Anyone holding a signed token can decode its header and payload. Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality. Encrypted JWTs use a different representation.

Common claims​

RFC 7519 defines these registered claims:

ClaimMeaning
issIssuer
subSubject, such as a user identifier
audIntended recipient or recipients
expExpiration time
nbfTime before which the token is not accepted
iatTime the token was issued
jtiToken identifier

The time claims use seconds since the Unix epoch. nbf is a timestamp, not a delay after issuance. Claim names are case-sensitive. The application or token profile determines which claims are required and how to interpret custom claims such as admin.

Using a token in an API​

An authentication service can issue a token after checking a user's credentials. A client can then present it to an API using the Bearer scheme:

Authorization: Bearer <access-token>

The API needs to validate the token before using its claims. For a signed access token, that includes checking the signature with an allowed algorithm and trusted key, then checking the expected issuer, audience and relevant time constraints. RFC 8725 covers JWT validation practices and common implementation failures.

A valid token isn't permission to do everything. The API still needs to decide whether the caller can perform the requested operation on the requested resource.

Authentication establishes who a caller is. Authorisation determines what that caller can do. A JWT can carry information used in those decisions; it doesn't replace them.

What JWTs don't solve​

Revocation and stale claims. If a user's permissions change, an already issued token may still contain the old values. Expiry limits its lifetime, but immediate revocation needs an additional mechanism, such as a server-side check. A jti value alone doesn't prevent replay.

Browser security. Token storage is a separate design choice. JWT doesn't prescribe local storage or cookies, and the format doesn't remove the risks of script access or cross-site requests.

Cross-origin access. Bearer tokens don't bypass CORS. A browser request with an Authorization header can require a preflight, and the server must allow the relevant origin and header.

Server-side state. An API may be able to validate a self-contained token without looking up a session on every request. That doesn't mean the whole application is stateless or never needs current permission data.

JWTs are useful when systems need to exchange verifiable claims. For a browser application, a server-side session may be simpler. Choose the authentication and session design first, then use a token format where it serves that design.

item.title: Hello, world
item.content:encoded:
Hello, world. 🌏

This is my first post. I've worked as a software developer in the UK since 2011, but until now I haven't written much about it.

I've learnt a lot from other people's blogs. I'd like to share some of what I've picked up and give something back.
